title: Jacob Beam on Hardin Creek
summary: Jacob Beam, a farmer and miller of German descent, settled on Hardin's Creek in Washington County, Kentucky, where the Beam whiskey line began.
bodyMarkdown:
Johannes Jacob Beam was of German descent; his family's surname, Böhm, became Beam in English ([Hardin's Creek: our story](https://www.beamdistilling.com/hardins-creek/our-story); [Wikipedia: Jim Beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beam)). According to the family's history, he farmed in Maryland before moving west to Kentucky in the late 1780s, and he brought a copper pot still with him ([Grokipedia: Jim Beam](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jim_Beam)). He settled on Hardin's Creek, a tributary of the Salt River, in what is now [Washington County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Washington_County,_Kentucky), where, the company says, the creek's water powered a mill that ground his corn ([Hardin's Creek: our story](https://www.beamdistilling.com/hardins-creek/our-story)). Company accounts give different years for when he arrived.

Corn grew well in Kentucky's new clearings, but the frontier had few roads. Hauling bulky grain overland or downriver to market cost more than the grain was worth. Distilling a surplus turned it into whiskey, which was smaller, kept for years and was easier to sell or trade. Western farmers had defended that same practice during the [Whiskey Rebellion](https://grokipedia.com/page/Whiskey_Rebellion) of 1794 in western Pennsylvania. This farm-surplus spirit is where [bourbon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bourbon_whiskey) began.

Family and company tradition holds that around 1795, after several good corn harvests, Jacob Beam sold his first barrel of whiskey, remembered as "Old Jake Beam" sour mash ([Jim Beam: Beam history](https://www.jimbeam.com/en-us/our-story/beam-history); [Hardin's Creek: our story](https://www.beamdistilling.com/hardins-creek/our-story)). No independent record of that sale survives, so the date is best read as the family's founding story, not a documented event.

Jacob Beam lived among other new arrivals. Nearby stood Hardin's Creek Meeting House, a Presbyterian congregation established by Virginia settlers in 1789; the settlement around it later grew into Lebanon ([KHS marker #867](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/259)). Other farmer-distillers worked the same country, among them [Basil Hayden](/stories/basil-haydens-high-rye-trail/) on Pottinger's Creek and [Jacob Spears](/stories/jacob-spears-early-bourbon-whiskey/) in Bourbon County.

The business passed down through Jacob's descendants. His son David Beam (1802–1854) took over in 1820, still making Old Jake Beam whiskey, and expanded the distillery as equipment improved. Under David M. Beam, who took over in the 1850s, the family whiskey became known as Old Tub, and from 1880 it was bottled and sold nationally under that name ([Beam founders history](https://founders.beamsuntory.com/dna/jimbeam); [Wikipedia: Jim Beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beam)). His son James B. "Jim" Beam (1864–1947) led the company into the 20th century ([Grokipedia: Jim Beam](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jim_Beam)).

[Prohibition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Prohibition_in_the_United_States) shut the distillery in 1919–1920. After repeal on December 5, 1933, Jim Beam and his son T. Jeremiah Beam rebuilt it at Clermont in Bullitt County, and the revived company's whiskey later took his name.

## Kentucky today

The Beam family name lives on in Kentucky bourbon. Hardin's Creek, the stream Jacob Beam settled on, gives its name to a modern line of rare releases from James B. Beam Distilling Co. The original farm site on Hardin's Creek is private land. Visitors can see the area from public roads, or tour the distillery at Clermont.
